newsitem.title: ZAIRE: As Zaire force takes shape,worry over armed Hutus.
newsitem.headline: As Zaire force takes shape,worry over armed Hutus.

text.p: The United States and Britain have signalled readiness to join a multinational force to save a million starving war refugees in Zaire, but the mission faces potential perils in dealing with armed Hutu hardliners.

A U.N. envoy negotiating a mandate for the force with Rwanda and Zaire, whose army is battling Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels, said on Wednesday it was unclear how the force could handle armed Hutus using refugees as a screen.
Most are former soldiers of the Rwanda Armed Forces (FAR) who fled with Hutu civilians after losing a civil war following the 1994 massacre of Tutsis in Rwanda.
The world community is eager to avoid a re-run of 1994 when it effectively fed and gave sanctuary to many of those responsible for the slaughter of an estimated 800,000 people, mainly Tutsis.
The Hutus fear revenge for the genocide and are apparently putting up a last stand at the teeming Mugunga refugee camp near Goma.
"We don't know what is the strength of the ex-FAR and the Interahamwe (Hutu miltia)," said United Nations envoy Raymond Chretien after talks in the Zaire capital Kinshasa on Wednesday.
"We don't know whether they will accept to be separated from their human shield," Chretien told reporters.
He said, however, that both Zaire and Rwanda are now agreed on the main objectives of the proposed international humanitarian intervention in the region.

"They are agreed...to help the Rwandan, Burundian or Zairean refugees on the ground on Zairean territory. They are agreed that this force should create the conditions for an eventual voluntary repatriation of the refugees to their countries of origin," he said.
"They are both agreed that if this force does not achieve the return of the refugees then it will have failed," he added.
Until Wednesday Zaire had insisted that any aid for Rwandan refugees should be distributed only in Rwanda as a way of encouraging the refugees to return home.
It also opposed any dealings between aid agencies and Tutsi rebels who seized Zaire's two eastern provinces bordering Rwanda since fighting erupted on October 18.
A government spokesman denounced a deal between aid agencies and rebels which allowed a first consignment of aid to enter the city of Goma on Monday as a violation of Zaire's sovereignty.
Chretien was unable to specify whether the proposed Canadian-led force would operate out of both Rwanda and Zaire.
But he said troops could be ready to act within a matter of days. Only a mandate from the Council was now needed.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said the U.S. commitment, which was expected to last about four months, involves dispatching 1,000 ground troops to the African nation. Several thousand additional troops would be sent to the region to help with support activities, he said.

"The president has decided that the United States is willing, in principle, to participate in a limited fashion in this mission as long as certain conditions are (respected)," McCurry said at a White House briefing.
Among the conditions he listed were that the mission would be of limited duration and involve a multinational force.
In London, Britain said it was ready to contribute troops but Prime Minister John Major said vital details about the international mission still needed to be worked out.

"Ministers agreed the UK should be ready to contribute constructively to the international response, including to a multinational force, providing a satisfactory plan can be worked out," a statement from Major's office said on Wednesday.
France which led the intervention lobby but which is seen by Rwanda as partisan in the Hutu-Tutsi conflict behind much of the bloodletting in Central Africa, welcomed the new commitments.
